title: Gulf Arabic grammar
about: Only what Saudi Arabic does differently from Modern Standard Arabic, in 16 short lessons: how it sounds, the words for what, where and why, how to say “not”, “want”, “will” and “still”, the verb endings, numbers and “if”. Everything else works as in Standard Arabic, so the Arabic grammar course comes first. Every example is Arabic as people in Riyadh say it, with vowel marks and a reading in Latin letters that shows the Saudi sounds (g for ق), and you can tap it to hear it.

lessons.title: Sound like Riyadh
lessons.summary: Say {{قَهْوَة}} “coffee” and {{قَال}} “he said” the way people in Riyadh do: the few sound changes that make Standard Arabic sound Saudi.
lessons.topic: Sounds: {{ق}} said g, {{ض}} said like {{ظ}}, hamza dropped, short vowels squeezed out

dialog.tr: What do you want? Coffee or tea?
Coffee, thank you.
Sure, I'll bring it now.

blocks.p: This course builds on Standard Arabic (MSA). It teaches only what is **different** in the Arabic spoken in Saudi Arabia, in the style of Riyadh and the central region, Najd: the variety heard most on Saudi TV and in Saudi offices. Everything not mentioned here works as in MSA: the letters, the roots, most words, {{عِنْدِي}} “I have”, and the order of words.

blocks.means: the everyday spoken Arabic of one region (here: Saudi Arabia, Riyadh style), as opposed to Modern Standard Arabic, the Arabic of books and the news.

blocks.p: **{{ق}} is said g.** In almost every everyday word, Saudis say {{ق}} like the g in “go”: {{قَال|gāl}} “he said”, {{قَهْوَة|gahwah}} “coffee”, {{قَرِيب|garīb}} “near”, {{قَلْب|galb}} “heart”. It is still **written** {{ق}}. Religious and formal words keep the standard q: {{الْقُرْآن|al-qurʾān}}, {{قَانُون|qānūn}} “law”.

**{{ث}} and {{ذ}} stay.** Unlike Cairo or Damascus, Saudis keep the “th” sounds of MSA: {{ثَلَاث|thalāth}} “three”, {{هَذَا|hādha}} “this”. **{{ض}} is said like {{ظ}}** (a heavy “dh”): {{أَبْيَض|abyaḍh}} “white”, {{ضَيْف|ḍhēf}} “guest”.

**Hamza mostly goes.** {{رَائِح}} becomes {{رَايِح|rāyiḥ}} “going”, {{جَاءَ}} becomes {{جَا|ja}} “he came”, {{سَمَاء}} becomes {{سَمَا|sama}} “sky”. And **short vowels drop out** where MSA has several in a row: {{كَتَبَتْ}} sounds {{كِتْبَت|kitbat}} “she wrote”, and {{يَكْتُبُ}} sounds {{يِكْتِب|yiktib}}. The ending {{ة}} is said -ah: {{سَاعَة|sāʿah}} “hour”.

blocks.tip: **Spelling.** Saudis write their dialect with ordinary Arabic letters, so a written word often looks just like MSA: only the sound changes. In this course the Latin reading under each example shows how it is said (g for {{ق}}, ē and ō for the vowels of {{بَيْت}} and {{يَوْم}}).

mistakes.why: In everyday words {{ق}} is said g.
The hamza of MSA becomes {{ي}} or disappears: {{رَايِح}}, {{جَا}}.

practice.q: How does someone from Riyadh say {{قَال}} “he said”?
practice.why: {{ق}} is said g, and the final vowel goes: gāl.

practice.q: Which sound do Saudis **keep**, unlike Egyptians?
Say “The house is near”, with a Saudi g.
Your turn: say three words with {{ق}} the Saudi way, for example {{قَهْوَة}}, {{قَرِيب}}, {{قَال}}.

lessons.title: Drop the endings
lessons.summary: Say {{بَيْت كْبِير}} “a big house” and {{رِيَالَيْن}} “two riyals” without the case endings and verb duals of MSA.
lessons.topic: No case endings or nunation; the dual only on nouns; plural verbs and adjectives for two

goal.tr: I have two boys, and they're at school.

dialog.tr: How many children do you have?
I have two boys and a girl.

dialog.t: مَا شَاء اللَّه! وَيْن هُمْ الْحِين؟
dialog.tr: How lovely! Where are they now?
The two boys went to school.

blocks.means: the short vowel at the end of an MSA word that shows its job in the sentence (-u, -a, -i, and -un, -an, -in): {{كِتَابٌ}}, {{كِتَابًا}}, {{كِتَابٍ}}.

blocks.p: **No case endings.** The dialect drops them all, and the -n of nunation too: MSA {{بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ}} is just {{بَيْت كْبِير|bēt kbīr}} “a big house”, whatever its place in the sentence. A few fixed words keep -an: {{شُكْرًا|shukran}} “thanks”, {{أَهْلًا|ahlan}} “hi”.

**The dual only on nouns.** Two of something is still -ēn ({{ـَيْن}}) on the noun: {{يَوْمَيْن|yōmēn}} “two days”, {{رِيَالَيْن|riyālēn}} “two riyals”, {{سَاعْتَيْن|sāʿtēn}} “two hours”. But verbs, adjectives and pronouns for two people are **plural**: {{الْوَلَدَيْن رَاحُوا|al-waladēn rāḥaw}} “the two boys went” (not {{ذَهَبَا}}), {{كِتَابَيْن حِلْوَيْن|kitābēn ḥilwīn}} “two nice books”.
**One ending, -ēn.** MSA has -āni and -ayni; Saudi Arabic has only -ēn, written {{ـَيْن}}: {{ثْنَيْن|thinēn}} “two”, {{شَهْرَيْن|shahrēn}} “two months”.

ex.tr: I stayed two days in Jeddah.
The two girls went to the market.

blocks.tip: Leaving the endings off is not careless speech: it is how every Arab speaks. Reading the news aloud, Saudis add the endings back; talking, they never do.

mistakes.why: No case endings or -un in the dialect.
The verb for two is plural: {{رَاحُوا}}.

practice.why: The dual ending is {{ـَيْن}} (-ēn) on the noun.
For two people the verb is plural.

practice.q: A colleague asks about your weekend.

lines.tr: How many days did you stay in Jeddah?
Only two days? That's not much!

practice.q: Your turn: say how many brothers and sisters you have, with the dual if it's two: {{عِنْدِي…}}

answers.tr: I have two brothers and a sister.

lessons.title: Say “we”, “you all” and “my, your”
lessons.summary: Use the Saudi pronouns, above all {{حِنَّا}} “we”, and the endings for “my, your, his”.
lessons.topic: The pronouns ({{حِنَّا}}, {{انْتُم}}, {{انْتِن}}, {{هِن}}) and the possessive endings ({{ـَه}} said -ah)

dialog.t: حِنَّا مِن الرِّيَاض. وِانْتُم مِن وَيْن؟
dialog.r: ḥinna min ar-riyāḍh. w-intum min wēn?
dialog.tr: We're from Riyadh. And where are you from?

dialog.t: حِنَّا مِن أَسْتُرَالْيَا، بَسّ سَاكْنِين هِنَا.
dialog.r: ḥinna min ustrālya, bass sāknīn hina.
dialog.tr: We're from Australia, but we live here.
Welcome! Is this your house?
Yes, and that's my brother's car.

blocks.p: **“We” is {{حِنَّا|ḥinna}}**, not {{نَحْنُ}}. You will also hear {{إِحْنَا|iḥna}} from other Saudis. The rest is close to MSA, without the final vowels: {{أَنَا|ana}}, {{انْتَ|inta}} (to a man), {{انْتِي|inti}} (to a woman), {{هُو|hu}}, {{هِي|hi}}.

**The plural keeps men and women apart.** Najdi Arabic still has a separate “you” and “they” for groups of women, like MSA: {{انْتُم|intum}} / {{انْتِن|intin}} “you all”, {{هُم|hum}} / {{هِن|hin}} “they”. There is no “you two” or “they two”: for two people, use the plural.

**The endings for “my, your, his”** are MSA's, without their last vowel. Two to listen for: “his” {{ـَه}} is said **-ah** ({{بَيْتَه|bētah}} “his house”), and “your” to a woman is said -ik ({{بَيْتِك|bētik}}); older Najdis say it -its. “My brother” is {{أَخُوي|akhūy}}, “my father” {{أَبُوي|abūy}}.

blocks.tip: {{أَبُوي}} and {{أَخُوي}} come from {{أَبُو}} and {{أَخُو}} + -y. In the same way Saudis say {{يُبَه|yuba}} “Dad!” and {{يُمَّه|yummah}} “Mum!” when they call their parents.

mistakes.why: There is no “you two”: use the plural {{انْتُم}}.

practice.q: You're talking to a group of women. Choose the word.
practice.why: Najdi keeps a “you all” for women: {{انْتِن}}.

practice.q: Your turn: say where you and your family are from, with {{حِنَّا}}.

answers.t: أَنَا مِن لَنْدَن، وْأَهْلِي مِن الْهِنْد.
answers.r: ana min landan, w-ahli min al-hind.
answers.tr: I'm from London, and my family is from India.

lessons.title: Ask what, why, where and how
lessons.summary: Ask {{وِشْ}} “what”, {{لَيْش}} “why”, {{وَيْن}} “where” and {{وِشْلُون}} “how”, the Saudi question words.

goal.tr: What's your name? And where are you from?

dialog.tr: Hello. What's your name?
Hello. My name's Tom.
How are you, Tom? Where do you live?

dialog.t: زَيْن، الْحَمْد لِلَّه. سَاكِن فِي الْعُلَيَّا.
dialog.r: zēn, al-ḥamdu lillah. sākin fi l-ʿulayya.
dialog.tr: Fine, thank God. I live in Olaya.

blocks.p: **What: {{وِشْ|wesh}}.** The most Saudi word of all. It goes where the answer would go, usually first: {{وِشْ تِبِي؟|wesh tibi?}} “What do you want?”, {{وِشْ هَذَا؟|wesh hādha?}} “What's this?”. “What's wrong?” is {{وِشْ فِيك؟|wesh fīk?}}. You will also hear {{إِيش|ēsh}} from people from Jeddah.

**Why, where, how.** {{لَيْش|lēsh}} “why” (from {{لِأَيِّ شَيْء}} “for what thing”), {{وَيْن|wēn}} “where”, {{مِنَيْن|minēn}} or {{مِن وَيْن|min wēn}} “from where”. “How” is {{كَيْف|kēf}} or {{وِشْلُون|weshlōn}}; “How are you?” is {{وِشْلُونِك؟|weshlōnak?}} (to a man), {{وِشْلُونِك؟|weshlōnik?}} (to a woman).
**No {{هَلْ}}.** A yes-or-no question is a statement said with a rising voice: {{انْتَ سْعُودِي؟|inta sʿūdi?}} “Are you Saudi?”

blocks.tip: {{وِشْ}} can join the next word: {{وِشْلُون}} is {{وِشْ}} + {{لُون}} “colour”, “what colour (state) are you?”.

practice.q: You meet a neighbour in the lift.

lines.why: {{وَيْن رَايِح}} is “where are you going?”: to work, {{الدَّوَام}}.

practice.q: Your turn: ask a new colleague three questions: their name, where they're from, where they live.

answers.t: وِشْ اسْمِك؟ مِن وَيْن انْتَ؟ وَيْن سَاكِن؟
answers.r: wesh ismak? min wēn inta? wēn sākin?
answers.tr: What's your name? Where are you from? Where do you live?

goal.tr: This one's mine, and that one's yours.

dialog.tr: Hello, what would you like?
How much is this bag?
This one's a hundred. And that one's fifty.
And these?
These are twenty, all of them.

blocks.p: **This:** {{هَذَا|hādha}} for a masculine noun, **{{هَذِي|hādhi}}** for a feminine one (not {{هَذِهِ}}). **These: {{هَذُولَا|hādhōla}}** (also {{هَذُولِي|hādhōli}}) for people and things, not {{هَؤُلَاءِ}}.
**That:** {{هَذَاك|hādhāk}} (masculine), {{هَذِيك|hādhīk}} (feminine), {{هَذُولَاك|hādhōlāk}} “those”. MSA's {{ذَلِكَ}} and {{تِلْكَ}} are not used in speech.

**{{هَالـ|hal-}} “this”.** In front of a noun, “this” is often just {{هَالـ}}, joined to it: {{هَالْبَيْت|hal-bēt}} “this house”, {{هَالْأَيَّام|hal-ayyām}} “these days”. It works for masculine, feminine and plural alike. The full form goes **before** a noun with {{الْـ}}: {{هَذَا الْبَيْت|hādha l-bēt}}.

ex.tr: These days the weather is hot.

blocks.tip: Short forms you will hear: {{ذَا|dha}} “this” and {{ذِي|dhi}} for {{هَذَا}} and {{هَذِي}}, as in {{وِشْ ذَا؟|wesh dha?}} “What's this?”.

practice.q: Say: “These days the weather is hot”, with {{هَالـ}}.
Your turn: point at three things around you and say what they are: {{هَذَا…}}, {{هَذِي…}}, {{هَذُولَا…}}

answers.t: هَذَا جَوَّالِي، وْهَذِي قَهْوَتِي، وْهَذُولَا كُتُبِي.
answers.r: hādha jawwāli, w-hādhi gahwati, w-hādhōla kutubi.
answers.tr: This is my phone, this is my coffee, and these are my books.

lessons.title: Say what isn't so
lessons.summary: Say {{مَا أَدْرِي}} “I don't know”, {{مُو زَيْن}} “not good” and {{مَانِي فَاضِي}} “I'm not free”.
lessons.topic: Negation: {{مَا}} with verbs, {{لَا}} in commands, {{مُو}} / {{مُوب}} / {{مَانِي}} with everything else

goal.tr: I don't know, honestly I'm not sure.

dialog.tr: Are you coming to the restaurant with us?
No, I'm not free today.
Why? That's not fair!
I've got work, and I haven't finished it.

blocks.p: **With a verb: {{مَا|ma}}**, for the past and the present alike: {{مَا رِحْت|ma riḥt}} “I didn't go”, {{مَا أَدْرِي|ma adri}} “I don't know”. MSA's {{لَمْ}}, {{لَنْ}} and {{لَا}} + present are not used. **Commands** keep {{لَا|lā}}: {{لَا تْرُوح|lā trūḥ}} “don't go”.

**With everything else: {{مُو|mū}}** (also {{مُوب|mūb}}, {{مُب|mub}}) in place of {{لَيْسَ}}: {{مُو زَيْن|mū zēn}} “not good”, {{مُو هِنَا|mū hina}} “not here”. Najdi Arabic also joins {{مَا}} to an ending: {{مَانِي|māni}} “I'm not”, {{مَاهُو|māhu}} / {{مَهُوب|mahūb}} “he isn't”, {{مَاهِي|māhi}} “she isn't”.

**Nobody, nothing, never.** {{مَحَد|maḥad}} “nobody” ({{مَا}} + {{أَحَد}}), {{وَلَا شَي|wala shay}} “nothing”, {{أَبَد|abad}} “not at all, never”. And “I don't know” has a short form everyone uses: {{مَدْرِي|madri}}.

ex.tr: I don't know where he went.

blocks.tip: Saudi negation has no extra -sh at the end as in Cairo: Riyadh says {{مَا شِفْتَه}}, never {{مَا شُفْتُوش}}.

practice.tr: I didn't go to work yesterday.

lines.tr: Where are you? Are you coming with us?

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you didn't do yesterday, with {{مَا}}.

answers.t: مَا رِحْت الدَّوَام، وْمَا شِفْت أَحَد.
answers.r: ma riḥt ad-dawām, w-ma shift aḥad.
answers.tr: I didn't go to work, and I didn't see anyone.

lessons.title: Say what there is
lessons.summary: Ask {{فِيه صَيْدَلِيَّة قَرِيبَة؟}} “Is there a chemist's nearby?” and answer {{إِيه فِيه}} or {{مَا فِيه}}.

dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there a chemist's nearby?
Yes, there's one next to the corner shop.
And is there parking?

dialog.t: لَا، مَا فِيه. بَسّ فِيه قِدَّام الْمَسْجِد.
dialog.r: lā, ma fīh. bass fīh giddām al-masjid.
dialog.tr: No, there isn't. But there is in front of the mosque.

blocks.p: **{{فِيه|fīh}} “there is, there are”** replaces MSA {{هُنَاكَ}} and {{يُوجَدُ}}. It never changes: {{فِيه مُشْكِلَة|fīh mushkilah}} “there's a problem”, {{فِيه نَاس|fīh nās}} “there are people”. **“There isn't”: {{مَا فِيه|ma fīh}}**. As a question, just raise your voice: {{فِيه أَحَد؟|fīh aḥad?}} “Is anyone there?”

Short answers: {{إِيه، فِيه|ēh, fīh}} “yes, there is”, {{لَا، مَا فِيه|lā, ma fīh}} “no, there isn't”. With people, {{مَحَد|maḥad}} “nobody” does the work of {{مَا فِيه أَحَد}}: {{مَحَد هِنَا|maḥad hina}} “nobody's here”.

ex.tr: There's no milk in the fridge.

blocks.tip: {{مَا فِيه مُشْكِلَة}} “no problem” and {{مَا فِيه دَاعِي|ma fīh dāʿi}} “there's no need” are among the phrases you'll hear most.

practice.tr: There's parking in front of the mosque.

practice.q: You knock at a friend's door.

lines.tr: No, nobody's here. They went to the market.

practice.tr: There's no milk in the fridge.

practice.q: Your turn: say what there is and isn't near your home, with {{فِيه}} and {{مَا فِيه}}.

answers.t: فِيه بَقَّالَة قَرِيبَة، بَسّ مَا فِيه مَطْعَم.
answers.r: fīh baggālah garībah, bass ma fīh maṭʿam.
answers.tr: There's a corner shop nearby, but there's no restaurant.

lessons.title: Count, pay and tell your age
lessons.summary: Say prices and ages: {{خَمْسْطَعَش رِيَال}} “fifteen riyals”, {{عِشْرِين سَنَة}} “twenty years”.
lessons.topic: Numbers: {{ثْنَيْن}}, {{ثَمَان}}; 11–19 end in {{ـطَعَش}}; {{مِيَّة}}; no case endings after numbers

dialog.tr: How much is the coffee?
The small one is twelve, the large one sixteen.
I want two small ones.
OK, twenty-four riyals.

blocks.p: **One to ten** are MSA's, said the Saudi way, without case endings: {{وَاحِد|wāḥid}}, {{ثْنَيْن|thnēn}} (feminine {{ثِنْتَيْن|thintēn}}), {{ثَلَاث|thalāth}}, {{أَرْبَع|arbaʿ}}, {{خَمْس|khams}}, {{سِتّ|sitt}}, {{سَبْع|sabʿ}}, {{ثَمَان|thamān}}, {{تِسْع|tisʿ}}, {{عَشْر|ʿashr}}. Counting out loud, or with no noun after them, they take -ah: {{ثَلَاثَة|thalāthah}}, {{أَرْبَعَة|arbaʿah}}. Before a noun, the short form and the plural: {{ثَلَاث سَاعَات|thalāth sāʿāt}} “three hours”.

**Eleven to nineteen** are one word ending in **-ṭaʿash** ({{ـطَعَش}}), from MSA {{عَشَرَ}}. After them, and after 20 and up, the noun is **singular**, as in MSA but without -an: {{خَمْسْطَعَش رِيَال|khamsṭaʿash riyāl}}, {{عِشْرِين سَنَة|ʿishrīn sanah}}.

**Tens and hundreds.** {{عِشْرِين|ʿishrīn}}, {{ثَلَاثِين|thalāthīn}}… as in MSA, with -īn only. A hundred is {{مِيَّة|miyyah}}, two hundred {{مِيتَيْن|mītēn}}, a thousand {{أَلْف|alf}}, two thousand {{أَلْفَيْن|alfēn}}. “And” goes between the parts, the units first: {{خَمْسَة وْعِشْرِين|khamsah w-ʿishrīn}} “25”.

ex.tr: This is a hundred and fifty.

blocks.tip: Prices are said with {{بْـ}} “for”: {{بْكَمْ؟|b-kam?}} “for how much?”, {{بْعَشْرَة|b-ʿashrah}} “for ten”. A riyal has 100 {{هَلَلَة|halalah}}.

mistakes.why: 11–19 are one word in {{ـطَعَش}}, and no -an on the noun.

practice.q: Your turn: say how old you are and how much your last coffee cost.

answers.t: عُمْرِي خَمْسَة وْعِشْرِين سَنَة، وِالْقَهْوَة كَانَت بْثَمَنْطَعَش رِيَال.
answers.r: ʿumri khamsah w-ʿishrīn sanah, w-al-gahwah kānat b-thamanṭaʿash riyāl.
answers.tr: I'm twenty-five, and the coffee was eighteen riyals.

lessons.title: Say what you want, can and must do
lessons.summary: {{أَبِي أَرُوح}} “I want to go”, {{مَا أَقْدَر}} “I can't”, {{لَازِم أَمْشِي}} “I have to leave”: with no {{أَنْ}} in between.
lessons.topic: {{أَبِي}} / {{تِبِي}} “want”, {{وَدِّي}} “I'd like”, {{أَقْدَر}} “I can”, {{لَازِم}} “must”, straight before the verb

goal.t: أَبِي أَرُوح، بَسّ لَازِم أَخَلِّص شُغْلِي.
goal.r: abi arūḥ, bass lāzim akhalliṣ shughli.
goal.tr: I want to go, but I have to finish my work.

dialog.tr: Do you want to come with us to the desert?
I'd love to, but I can't today.
Why?
I have to take my mother to the hospital.

blocks.p: **“Want”: {{أَبِي|abi}}**, from the verb {{بِغَى}}: {{أَبِي|abi}} “I want”, {{تِبِي|tibi}} “you want” (to a woman {{تِبِين|tibīn}}), {{يِبِي|yibi}} “he wants”, {{نِبِي|nibi}} “we want”, {{تِبُون|tibūn}} “you all want”, {{يِبُون|yibūn}} “they want”. With a thing: {{أَبِي مُويَة|abi mōyah}} “I want water”. (People from Jeddah say {{أَبْغَى|abgha}}.)

**No {{أَنْ}}.** In MSA {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ}}; in Saudi Arabic the second verb follows straight on, in its plain present form: {{أَبِي أَرُوح|abi arūḥ}} “I want to go”. The same after {{وَدِّي|waddi}} “I'd like” (literally “my wish”), {{أَقْدَر|agdar}} “I can”, {{لَازِم|lāzim}} “I must, I have to”, and {{الْمَفْرُوض|al-mafrūḍh}} “I'm supposed to”.
**“Is there time?”** Saudis ask {{يِمْدِيك؟|yimdīk?}} “do you have time (to)?”, and answer {{مَا يِمْدِينِي|ma yimdīni}} “I won't make it”.

ex.tr: What do you want to eat?

blocks.tip: {{أَبِي}} also means “my father” in MSA, but in a Saudi sentence it is almost always “I want”. “My father” is {{أَبُوي|abūy}}.

practice.tr: Do you want to eat something?

practice.q: A colleague invites you to lunch.

lines.tr: Do you want to have lunch with us?

lines.why: No {{أَنْ}}: {{وَدِّي}} on its own is “I'd love to”.

practice.q: Your turn: say one thing you want to do this week and one thing you have to do.

answers.t: أَبِي أَرُوح الْبَرّ، بَسّ لَازِم أَدْرِس.
answers.r: abi arūḥ al-barr, bass lāzim adris.
answers.tr: I want to go to the desert, but I have to study.

lessons.title: Say whose it is: “It's mine”
lessons.summary: {{السَّيَّارَة حَقِّي}} “The car is mine”, {{الْجَوَّال حَقّ أَخُوي}} “It's my brother's phone”.

goal.tr: This phone is mine, not yours.

dialog.tr: Whose is this bag?
My sister's. And that one's mine.
And the key?
The key is for the car.

blocks.p: **{{حَقّ|ḥagg}} “belonging to”.** MSA puts the owner straight after the thing ({{سَيَّارَةُ أَخِي}}); Saudi Arabic can do that too ({{سَيَّارَة أَخُوي|sayyārat akhūy}}), but very often uses {{حَقّ}} in between: {{السَّيَّارَة حَقّ أَخُوي|as-sayyārah ḥagg akhūy}}. With an ending it is “mine, yours…”: {{حَقِّي|ḥaggi}}, {{حَقَّك|ḥaggak}}.

**It is useful when the thing has “the”**, or when you answer “whose?”: {{حَقّ مِن؟|ḥagg min?}} “whose?”, {{حَقِّي|ḥaggi}} “mine”. And {{حَقّ}} also means **“for”**: {{هَذَا حَقَّك|hādha ḥaggak}} “this is for you”, {{الْمِفْتَاح حَقّ الْبَاب|al-miftāḥ ḥagg al-bāb}} “the key for the door”.

blocks.tip: Kuwaitis and Emiratis say {{مَال|māl}} for the same thing ({{مَالِي|māli}} “mine”); in Riyadh you will mostly hear {{حَقّ}}.

practice.q: You find a phone on the table.

lines.tr: I don't know, it's not mine.

practice.q: Your turn: point at three things and say whose they are, with {{حَقّ}}.

answers.t: الْجَوَّال حَقِّي، وِالسَّيَّارَة حَقّ أَبُوي، وِالْكِتَاب حَقّ أُخْتِي.
answers.r: al-jawwāl ḥaggi, w-as-sayyārah ḥagg abūy, w-al-kitāb ḥagg ukhti.
answers.tr: The phone is mine, the car is my dad's, and the book is my sister's.

lessons.title: Say what you do, and tell people what to do
lessons.summary: {{أَشْرَب قَهْوَة كِلّ يَوْم}} “I drink coffee every day”, {{وِشْ تِسَوِّي؟}} “What do you do?”, {{تَعَال!}} “Come here!”
lessons.topic: The present without endings or moods ({{يِكْتِب}}, {{تِكْتِبِين}}, {{يِكْتِبُون}}); {{سَوَّى}} “do”; commands and {{خَلّنَا}} “let's”

goal.t: أَصْحَى بَدْرِي وْأَشْرَب قَهْوَة كِلّ يَوْم.
goal.r: aṣḥa badri w-ashrab gahwah kill yōm.
goal.tr: I get up early and drink coffee every day.

dialog.tr: What do you do in the morning?
I go to work, and I come back at three.
And then?
I have lunch and rest. Come over tomorrow!

blocks.p: **The present is MSA's, without its last vowel.** The letter in front still says who: {{أَكْتِب|aktib}} “I write”, {{تِكْتِب|tiktib}} “you write”, {{يِكْتِب|yiktib}} “he writes”, {{نِكْتِب|niktib}} “we write”. In Riyadh the front vowel is i ({{يِـ}}, {{تِـ}}, {{نِـ}}), except a- for “I”. The endings {{ـِين}} (to a woman) and {{ـُون}} (plural) stay, and groups of women have {{ـِن}}: {{تِكْتِبِين|tiktibīn}}, {{يِكْتِبُون|yiktibūn}}, {{يِكْتِبِن|yiktibin}}.

**No moods.** MSA's -a and short forms ({{أَنْ يَكْتُبَ}}, {{لَمْ يَكْتُبْ}}) are gone: the same form is used everywhere. And unlike Cairo or Damascus, Riyadh puts **no {{بِـ}}** in front of the everyday present: {{بِـ}} means “will” (a later lesson).
**“Do, make” is {{سَوَّى|sawwa}}**, present {{يِسَوِّي|yisawwi}}, not {{فَعَلَ}}: {{وِشْ تِسَوِّي؟|wesh tisawwi?}} “What are you doing?”, {{أَسَوِّي قَهْوَة|asawwi gahwah}} “I'm making coffee”.

**Commands** are the present without its front letter: {{تِكْتِب}} → {{اكْتِب|iktib}} “write!”, {{تِشْرَب}} → {{اشْرَب|ishrab}} “drink!”. “Don't” is {{لَا}} + the present: {{لَا تِتْأَخَّر|lā titʾakhkhar}} “don't be late”. **“Let's”**: {{خَلّنَا|khallna}} + the “we” form, or {{يَلَّا|yalla}}: {{خَلّنَا نْرُوح|khallna nrūḥ}}, {{يَلَّا نِمْشِي|yalla nimshi}}.

ex.tr: My sister studies at the university.

blocks.tip: {{تَفَضَّل|tafaḍḍal}} (to a woman {{تَفَضَّلِي}}) is the polite “please, go ahead, have some” that goes with any offer.

mistakes.why: In Riyadh {{بِـ}} means “will”; the everyday present has no {{بِـ}}.

practice.q: You're talking to a woman. Choose the word.
practice.why: To a woman the present ends in {{ـِين}}.

practice.q: How do you say “Let's go” in Riyadh?
Tell a group of friends to come. Choose the word.
A neighbour asks about your day.

lines.why: The present, with no {{بِـ}}, for what you do.

practice.q: Your turn: say three things you do every morning.

answers.tr: I wake up, drink coffee and go to work.

lessons.title: Say what you're doing right now
lessons.summary: {{قَاعِد أَطْبَخ}} “I'm cooking”, {{أَنَا رَايِح الْبَيْت}} “I'm going home”.

goal.t: مَا أَقْدَر أَكَلِّمِك الْحِين، قَاعِد أَسُوق.
goal.r: ma agdar akallmak al-ḥīn, gāʿid asūg.
goal.tr: I can't talk to you now, I'm driving.

dialog.tr: Where are you? What are you doing?
I'm studying in my room.
And your brother?
He's going to the mosque, and he's coming back in a bit.

blocks.means: a verb used like an adjective: {{رَايِح}} “going”, {{جَاي}} “coming”, {{قَاعِد}} “sitting”. It agrees with the person: -ah for a woman, -īn for a group.

blocks.p: **{{قَاعِد|gāʿid}} + present = “-ing”.** {{قَاعِد}} means “sitting”, and in front of a present verb it says the action is going on now: {{قَاعِد أَكْتِب|gāʿid aktib}} “I'm writing”. It agrees with the person: {{قَاعْدَة|gāʿdah}} (a woman), {{قَاعْدِين|gāʿdīn}} (a group). The plain present can also mean “-ing”: {{وِشْ تِسَوِّي؟|wesh tisawwi?}} “what are you doing?”. You'll also hear {{جَالِس|jālis}} in the same way.

**Going and coming** use a participle on its own: {{أَنَا رَايِح|ana rāyiḥ}} “I'm going”, {{هِي رَايْحَة|hi rāyḥah}} “she's going”, {{حِنَّا جَايِين|ḥinna jāyīn}} “we're coming”. Where to, with no {{إِلَى}}: {{رَايِح الْبَيْت|rāyiḥ al-bēt}} “going home”.

blocks.tip: {{قَاعِد}} + present can also mean “keeps doing”: {{قَاعِد يِتَّصِل كِلّ شْوَيّ|gāʿid yittaṣil kill shway}} “he keeps calling every five minutes”.

practice.q: Your turn: say what you and two people near you are doing right now.

answers.t: أَنَا قَاعِد أَدْرِس، وْأُخْتِي قَاعْدَة تِشُوف التِّلْفِزْيُون.
answers.r: ana gāʿid adris, w-ukhti gāʿdah tishūf at-tilifizyōn.
answers.tr: I'm studying, and my sister is watching TV.

lessons.title: Talk about your plans
lessons.summary: {{بَرُوح بَاكِر}} “I'll go tomorrow”, {{بَتِّصِل فِيك}} “I'll call you”.

goal.t: بَتِّصِل فِيك بَاكِر، إِنْ شَاء اللَّه.
goal.r: battiṣil fīk bākir, in shāʾ allah.
goal.tr: I'll call you tomorrow, God willing.

dialog.tr: What will you do in the holidays?
I'll travel to AlUla with my friends.
Nice! Will you go by car?
No, we'll go by plane.

blocks.p: **{{بِـ|b-}} + present = “will”.** Instead of MSA {{سَـ}} or {{سَوْفَ}}, Riyadh puts {{بِـ}} in front of the present: {{تِرُوح}} → {{بِتْرُوح|bitrūḥ}} “you'll go”, {{نِرُوح}} → {{بِنْرُوح|binrūḥ}} “we'll go”, {{يِجِي}} → {{بِيْجِي|bīji}} “he'll come”. With “I” it joins the a-: {{أَرُوح}} → {{بَرُوح|barūḥ}} “I'll go”.

**{{رَاح|rāḥ}}** + present means “will” too, especially among young people: {{رَاح أَسَافِر|rāḥ asāfir}}. **“Won't”** is {{مَا}} + the future: {{مَا بَرُوح|ma barūḥ}} or {{مَا رَاح أَرُوح|ma rāḥ arūḥ}} “I won't go”. There is no {{لَنْ}}.

blocks.tip: Plans almost always end with {{إِنْ شَاء اللَّه|in shāʾ allah}} “God willing”; Saudis say it whether or not they're sure.

practice.q: A friend asks about the weekend.

lines.tr: Will you come to dinner on Thursday?
Great! And bring your friends with you.

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you'll do this weekend and one you won't.

answers.t: بَزُور أَهْلِي، وْبِنْرُوح الْمَطْعَم، بَسّ مَا بَشْتَغِل.
answers.r: bazūr ahli, w-binrūḥ al-maṭʿam, bass ma bashtaghil.
answers.tr: I'll visit my family and we'll go to a restaurant, but I won't work.

lessons.title: Say what happened
lessons.summary: {{رِحْت}} “I went”, {{جَا}} “he came”, {{كِتْبَت}} “she wrote”, {{شِفْتُوا}} “you all saw”: the Saudi past endings.
lessons.topic: The past: endings without final vowels ({{ـْت}}, {{ـتِي}}, {{ـنَا}}, {{ـتُوا}}, {{ـُوا}}, {{ـِن}}); {{جَا}}, {{جِيت}}; object endings

goal.tr: Yesterday we went to the desert and saw the dunes.

dialog.tr: What did you all do yesterday?
We went on a desert picnic, and my sister came with us.
Nice! Did you have a good time?
Yes, but we got back late.

blocks.p: **The past works as in MSA, without the final vowels**, and three endings change. “You” to a woman is **-ti** ({{كِتَبْتِي|kitabti}}), “you all” is **-tu** ({{كِتَبْتُوا|kitabtu}}, not {{كَتَبْتُمْ}}), and “they” is **-u / -aw** ({{كِتْبُوا|kitbu}}). “I” and “you” to a man sound the same: {{كِتَبْت|kitabt}}. As in the present, groups of women have their own forms: {{كِتَبْتِن|kitabtin}} “you (women)”, {{كِتْبِن|kitbin}} “they (women)”.

**Verbs with a long vowel** shorten it before an ending, as in MSA: {{رَاح|rāḥ}} “he went” → {{رِحْت|riḥt}} “I went”; {{شَاف|shāf}} → {{شِفْت|shift}}. “Come” has lost its hamza: {{جَا|ja}} “he came”, {{جَات|jat}} “she came”, {{جِيت|jīt}} “I came”, {{جَوْا|jaw}} “they came”. And “his” on a verb is -ah: {{شِفْتَه|shiftah}} “I saw him”.

ex.tr: I went to the market and bought an abaya.
I haven't seen him for ages.
The guests came and had dinner.

blocks.tip: {{سَوَّى}} “do” in the past: {{سَوَّيْت|sawwēt}} “I did”, {{سَوَّيْتُوا|sawwētu}} “you all did”: the ē of {{ـيْت}} is the Saudi vowel of {{بَيْت}}.

practice.q: You're asking a group. Choose the word.
practice.tr: What did you all do yesterday?

practice.why: {{جِيت}}: I or you (a man) came; “he came” is {{جَا}}.

practice.q: A colleague asks about your weekend.

lines.tr: Where did you go at the weekend?
Nice! Did you have a good time?

practice.tr: I haven't seen him for ages.

practice.q: Your turn: say three things you did yesterday.

answers.t: صِحِيت بَدْرِي، وْرِحْت الدَّوَام، وْتَعَشَّيْت مَع أَهْلِي.
answers.r: ṣiḥīt badri, w-riḥt ad-dawām, w-taʿashshēt maʿ ahli.
answers.tr: I woke up early, went to work and had dinner with my family.

lessons.title: Say “just”, “still”, “not yet” and “not any more”
lessons.summary: {{تَوْنِي جِيت}} “I've just arrived”, {{لِلْحِين نَايِم}} “he's still asleep”, {{مَا عَاد}} “not any more”.
lessons.topic: Time words: {{تَوّ}} + ending “just”, {{لِلْحِين}} / {{بَعَد}} “still”, {{لِلْحِين مَا}} “not yet”, {{مَا عَاد}} “no longer”

goal.t: تَوْنِي صَاحِي، وْلِلْحِين مَا شِرِبْت قَهْوَتِي.
goal.r: tōni ṣāḥi, w-lil-ḥīn ma shiribt gahwati.
goal.tr: I've only just woken up, and I still haven't had my coffee.

dialog.tr: Has Khalid arrived?
No, he hasn't arrived yet.
And Fahad?

dialog.t: فَهَد تَوَّه طَالِع. مَا عَاد يِجْلِس مَعَنَا.
dialog.r: fahad tawwah ṭāliʿ. ma ʿād yijlis maʿana.
dialog.tr: Fahad has just left. He doesn't sit with us any more.

blocks.p: Najdi Arabic has a set of small words that place an action in time, where MSA uses {{قَدْ}}, {{مَا زَالَ}} or {{لَمْ… بَعْدُ}}. **“Just”: {{تَوّ|taww}} + an ending**, before a past verb or a participle: {{تَوْنِي جِيت|tōni jīt}} “I've just come”, {{تَوَّه رَاح|tawwah rāḥ}} “he's just gone”, {{تَوْهَا صَاحْيَة|tōha ṣāḥyah}} “she's just woken up”.

**“Still”: {{لِلْحِين|lil-ḥīn}}** (“up to now”) or {{بَعَد|baʿad}} + ending: {{لِلْحِين نَايِم|lil-ḥīn nāyim}}, {{بَعَدْه نَايِم|baʿadah nāyim}} “he's still asleep”. **“Not yet”: {{لِلْحِين مَا}}** or {{مَا بَعَد}} + past: {{لِلْحِين مَا جَا|lil-ḥīn ma ja}} “he hasn't come yet”. **“Not any more”: {{مَا عَاد|ma ʿād}}** + present: {{مَا عَاد أَدَخِّن|ma ʿād adakhkhin}} “I don't smoke any more”.

ex.tr: I haven't finished the work yet.
My dad is still at work.
I don't like sweets any more.

blocks.tip: {{تَوّ}} takes the endings of “my, his”: {{تَوْنِي|tōni}} “I just”, {{تَوَّك|tawwak}} “you just”, {{تَوَّه|tawwah}} “he just”, {{تَوْنَا|tōna}} “we just”. {{تَوَّك تِذْكُر؟|tawwak tidhkur?}} is a teasing “you've only just remembered?”.

practice.tr: I've just come back from work.

practice.q: Your mother asks about your brother.

practice.tr: My dad is still at work.

practice.q: Your turn: say something you've just done, something you haven't done yet, and something you don't do any more.

answers.t: تَوْنِي مِتْغَدِّي، وْلِلْحِين مَا ذَاكَرْت، وْمَا عَاد أَشْرَب بِبْسِي.
answers.r: tōni mitghaddi, w-lil-ḥīn ma dhākart, w-ma ʿād ashrab bibsi.
answers.tr: I've just had lunch, I haven't studied yet, and I don't drink Pepsi any more.

lessons.title: Join your ideas: if, because, until, when
lessons.summary: {{لَوْ تِبِي، تَعَال}} “If you want, come”, {{اللِّي}} “who, which”, {{عَشَان}} “because”, {{لَيْن}} “until”, {{يَوْم}} “when”.

goal.t: لَوْ تِبِي، تَعَال عِنْدَنَا يَوْم تِخَلِّص.
goal.r: law tibi, taʿāl ʿindana yōm tikhalliṣ.
goal.tr: If you want, come over when you finish.

dialog.tr: Do you know the man who came yesterday?
Yes, he's my brother's friend. Why?

dialog.t: نَسَى جَوَّالَه عِنْدِي. لَوْ تِشُوفَه، قُل لَه.
dialog.r: nisa jawwālah ʿindi. law tishūfah, gul lah.
dialog.tr: He left his phone at my place. If you see him, tell him.
Sure, I'll call him now.

blocks.p: **“If”: {{لَوْ|law}}** is used for real plans as well as for imagined ones, where MSA keeps {{إِذَا}} for real ones: {{لَوْ تِبِي، تَعَال|law tibi, taʿāl}} “if you want, come”. {{إِذَا|idha}} is heard too: {{إِذَا وَصَلْت دِقّ عَلَيّ|idha waṣalt digg ʿalayy}} “when you arrive, call me”. For something that didn't happen, {{لَوْ}} … {{كَان}}: {{لَوْ دِرِيت كَان جِيت|law dirīt kān jīt}} “if I'd known, I'd have come”.

**{{اللِّي|illi}} “who, which, that”**, the same word for everyone, in place of {{الَّذِي}}, {{الَّتِي}}, {{الَّذِينَ}}: {{الرِّجَّال اللِّي جَا|ar-rijjāl illi ja}} “the man who came”, {{الْبَنَات اللِّي شِفْتِهِن|al-banāt illi shifthin}} “the girls I saw”. On its own it means “what, whoever”: {{اللِّي تِبِيه|illi tibīh}} “whatever you want”.

ex.tr: I was late because of the traffic.
Wait for me until I come.
When I arrived, they were asleep.
Do you want tea or coffee?

ex.t: هَذَا الْكِتَاب اللِّي قِلْت لَك عَنَّه.
ex.r: hādha l-kitāb illi gilt lak ʿannah.
ex.tr: This is the book I told you about.

blocks.tip: {{يَوْم}} “day” works as “when” for the past: {{يَوْم كِنْت صْغِير|yōm kint ṣghīr}} “when I was little”.

mistakes.tr: Wait for me until I come.

practice.tr: The girl I saw is Saad's sister.
Do you want tea or coffee?

options: If I'd known, I'd have come.

practice.q: A friend is waiting for you.

lines.tr: Where are you? Why are you late?
OK, I'll wait for you until you get here.

practice.q: Your turn: say what you'll do if you're free this weekend, and why.

answers.t: لَوْ أَنَا فَاضِي، بَرُوح الْبَرّ عَشَان الْجَوّ حِلْو.
answers.r: law ana fāḍhi, barūḥ al-barr ʿashān al-jaww ḥilw.
answers.tr: If I'm free, I'll go to the desert because the weather is nice.
